summary: A 4-minute journey: how fingerprints form before birth and why even identical twins differ; how phone sensors read them (optical photo, capacitive electricity, ultrasonic sound); why a dead finger usually fails (no blood flow, cooling, drying and wrinkling skin, loss of conductance, plus phone rules like the iPhone's 48-hour passcode rule); and the twist that a very recently deceased finger can sometimes still work, which is why police have even tried 3D-printed fingertips.
audience: Curious Pakistani smartphone users aged 15-35 on Facebook who wonder how everyday tech works

facts.fact: Fingerprint ridges form before birth, mostly between about the 13th and 19th week of pregnancy, and stay the same for life.
Even identical twins, who share the same genes, have different fingerprints, because tiny conditions in the womb (position, finger growth, contact with fluid) shape the fine details.
Most smartphone fingerprint sensors identify a finger through electrical conductance rather than by taking a photo.
facts.source: Live Science (Anil Jain, Michigan State University)

facts.fact: A capacitive sensor is a grid of tiny cells; fingerprint ridges touch the sensor and give a stronger electrical reading than the valleys, which leave a small air gap, so the chip builds a map of the print.
Optical fingerprint sensors light up the finger and take a picture of it; they are cheaper and can sit under the screen.
facts.source: Android Authority: How fingerprint scanners work

facts.fact: Capacitive sensors use an array of extremely tiny capacitors that each hold a small electrical charge, and they are harder to fool than simple optical ones.
facts.source: Android Authority: How fingerprint scanners work

facts.fact: Ultrasonic sensors, found mainly in premium phones, send sound waves into the finger and measure the echo to build a 3D map of ridges and pores.
facts.source: Android Authority / iFixit: How ultrasonic fingerprint sensors work

facts.fact: Many sensors also try to check that a finger is real and alive (liveness detection), for example by its electrical or physical properties.
facts.source: arXiv review: Fingerprint-based authentication, liveness detection (2020); capacitive sensor patents

facts.fact: Fingerprint expert Anil Jain says it gets more difficult to unlock a phone with fingertips the longer a person has been dead.
Jain explained that without blood flow the fingers can start to wrinkle or shrivel, which changes the print the sensor sees.
facts.source: Live Science / Fortune coverage quoting Anil Jain

facts.fact: Jain also said that if a person has only recently died, it is possible to unlock a phone with their finger.
Scientists are not sure exactly how long after death the skin stops conducting electricity well enough for a sensor.
iPhones ask for the passcode instead of Touch ID if the phone has not been unlocked for more than 48 hours, after a restart, or after five failed fingerprint attempts.
facts.source: Apple Support: If Touch ID isn't working; Apple Platform Security guide

facts.fact: In 2016, US police asked Jain's lab to make 3D-printed fingertip copies from a murder victim's fingerprints to try to unlock his phone.
Your fingerprint pattern itself does not disappear at death; the problem for phone sensors is the skin's changing electrical and physical condition.

Any step-by-step advice on unlocking someone else's or a deceased person's phone
Graphic or gory depictions of bodies or severed fingers
Naming specific criminal cases or victims sensationally
Claiming all phones work the same way (optical and ultrasonic sensors also exist)
